summary: For ages 6-7, learners move among three representations of an addition/subtraction situation — a real-world story, a bar or part-whole drawing, and a symbolic number sentence — and explain how each connects to the others, saying what every number stands for. Two priorities drive the design: (1) the bar model is used to expose STRUCTURE (which quantity is the whole, which are the parts, where the unknown sits), not as a computing trick, and a single part-whole bar can be matched by several correct sentences (a=b+c, a=c+b, a−b=c, a−c=b); comparison bars serve the distinct 'how many more' type of situation. (2) The equals sign must be built as RELATIONAL ('the same amount on both sides'), because children very commonly read '=' as 'work out the answer' and will write compute-left-to-right sentences regardless of structure. True/false and open number sentences with the unknown in varied positions are the documented remedy; simply telling children '= means the same as' is reported insufficient on its own.
misconceptions: Reads '=' as 'work out the answer' (operational), so accepts or writes left-to-right computes like 8 + 4 = □ + 5 → 12 regardless of the structure
Grabs the two numbers in a story and adds them without asking which is the whole and which is a part
Ignores 'altogether'/total language when deciding what to combine
Can produce a matching sentence but cannot say what each number represents in the story

activities.title: Build the bar from the story, then write the sentence
steps: Read a story such as: '6 red apples, and some green apples, 10 apples altogether.'
Build a part-whole bar: first decide and label which quantity is the WHOLE, then place the known part, then mark the missing part with '?'.
Notice the classic error — putting 6 and 10 side by side as two parts — and correct it by recognising that 10 is the whole, 6 is a part, and the green apples are the missing part.
Write a matching number sentence (6 + ? = 10) and then write at least one other correct form for the same bar (e.g. 10 − 6 = ?).
Say aloud what each number in the sentence stands for in the story.

For a separate 'how many more' story with its own numbers (e.g. 'Tom has 5 stickers and Mia has 8 stickers — how many more does Mia have?'), build a COMPARISON bar instead, lining up the two amounts to show the difference, and write a matching sentence.
activities.insight: A part-whole bar shows the structure of a situation — which quantity is the whole and which are the parts — so you must identify the whole before deciding what to add, and one bar can be matched by several correct sentences (adding or subtracting). A comparison bar is a different representation that suits 'how many more' situations by lining up two amounts to show the difference between them.

activities.title: True/false and balance: '=' means 'the same as'
steps: Decide whether sentences are true or false: 8 = 8; 7 = 3 + 4; 8 + 4 = 12 + 5; 8 + 4 = 7 + 5.
Solve open sentences with the unknown in varied positions: □ = 9 + 5, 7 + □ = 6 + 4, 8 + 4 = □ + 5.
For 8 + 4 = □ + 5, try putting 12 in the box, check whether both sides are really equal, and adjust until they match (7).
Explain for each: how do you decide whether the two sides are the same amount?
activities.insight: The equals sign means 'the same amount on both sides', not 'the answer comes next'; so you cannot just copy the left-hand total into the box — you must make both sides equal.

activities.title: Explain-why with a study partner
steps: Consider a partner who says: 'The story has 6 red and 10 altogether, so I wrote 6 + 10 = 16 — good match?'
Decide whether this matches the story and say why or why not, naming what 10 is in the story (the whole).
When you write or accept a sentence, point at each number and state what it represents in the story.
Respond to a follow-up: 'Could you match the same story using take-away instead of add? Why does that work too?'
activities.insight: Explaining the connection out loud — naming the whole, the parts, and what each symbol stands for — is part of understanding, not an extra; a tempting-but-wrong sentence can be rejected with a structural reason.

activities.title: Read the links both ways (worked example / warm-up)
steps: Study a matched triple — the story, the bar, and the equation — and tap or point to show which part of the bar and which number corresponds to each part of the story.
Go in more than one direction: not only story→sentence, but bar→story and equation→bar, saying what matches what.
As a quick warm-up, pick which of several sentences matches a given bar, then justify the choice.
activities.insight: Representations should be read for meaning in both directions, and a correct matching sentence can be recognised and defended by its structure, not by grabbing the visible numbers.

checkQuestion: Here's a story: there are 6 red apples and some green apples, and 10 apples altogether. A classmate wrote this to match the story: 6 + 10 = 16. Do you think that matches the story? Talk me through it — what does each number stand for, and if it doesn't match, what would you write instead and why?
checkAnswer: No single scored answer — listen for the child recognising that 10 is the WHOLE (not a part to add), mapping 6 and the unknown green apples to the parts, and offering a structurally faithful sentence (6 + □ = 10, or 10 − 6 = □) while reading '=' as 'the same amount on both sides', not 'the answer goes here'.
